mcqs.question: What specifically makes a domain model "anemic"?
options: It uses inheritance instead of composition to represent related entities
It stores data in a relational database instead of an in-memory cache
It has fewer than five fields, making it too small to hold real behavior
Its entities hold only fields, getters, and setters, while all the rules governing them live in separate service classes
mcqs.explanation: Anemic is specifically about behavior location: the entity is a passive data bag and every rule about it lives outside, in services. It has nothing to do with inheritance vs composition, storage technology, or field count — a two-field or a twenty-field class can be equally anemic.

mcqs.question: Anemic models pass their tests and ship features. Why are they still considered an anti-pattern?
options: Because they run slower at runtime than rich models
Because they are incompatible with most database ORMs
Because the same rule about the entity tends to get reimplemented slightly differently across multiple services, drifting out of sync over time
Because unit testing frameworks cannot test anemic classes at all
mcqs.explanation: The real cost is rule duplication and drift — without a single owning object, the same check gets reimplemented in multiple services and slowly diverges. There's no inherent runtime speed penalty, no ORM incompatibility, and anemic classes are actually easy to unit test in isolation — the problem is where the logic lives, not testability of the data class itself.

mcqs.question: After moving `canCancel()` onto `Order` itself, what concretely changes for `RefundService` and the admin panel?
options: They still each write their own cancellability logic, just calling a helper function instead of duplicating it
They call `order.canCancel()` directly, so there's exactly one place the cancellation rule can drift out of sync with itself
They no longer need to reference the `Order` class at all
They must now subclass `Order` to access the cancellation logic
mcqs.explanation: The point of the refactor is consolidation: every caller now defers to the entity's own method instead of independently computing the same date/status logic. They still reference Order directly (correctly), no subclassing is introduced, and the fix isn't a shared helper function sitting outside the entity — it's the entity owning the rule itself.

mcqs.question: According to the testability comparison, what can you do with a rich `Order.canCancel()` that's harder with the anemic version?
options: Run the application in production without any test suite at all
Avoid writing any unit tests, since the logic is considered self-evidently correct
Skip code review for changes to the cancellation rule
Unit-test the rule directly on the entity, with no service class or mocks required to exercise it
mcqs.explanation: With the rule on the entity, a test can call `order.canCancel()` on a plain object with no service dependencies or mocking. None of the other options describe a real testability benefit — rich models still need tests, code review, and a production test suite just like anemic ones.

mcqs.question: A team decides every rule that ever touches `Order` — pricing math, shipping-label formatting, tax lookups, email copy — should become a method on `Order`. What's the risk?
options: There's no risk; a domain model can never have too much behavior on it
It will make the class impossible to compile due to method count limits
It turns `Order` into a differently-shaped God Object, giving one class many unrelated reasons to change and violating single responsibility
It automatically improves testability regardless of what the methods do
mcqs.explanation: Rich means owning the entity's own invariants, not absorbing every concern that mentions it — piling on unrelated responsibilities (formatting, tax lookups, email copy) recreates a God Object under a different name. There's no compiler method-count limit in practice, and cramming in unrelated logic actually hurts testability and cohesion rather than helping it.

mcqs.question: Why shouldn't Order.cancel() directly reach into and modify a Customer entity or Inventory records, according to the aggregate boundary concept?
options: Those entities are outside Order's aggregate boundary — an entity should directly touch only the small set of related objects it keeps consistent in one transaction, and delegate cross-aggregate coordination to an application service
Java and most ORMs technically forbid one entity's method from referencing another entity at all
It's fine to reach into any entity directly, as long as the method is named clearly
Aggregate boundaries only matter for read operations, never for methods that change state
mcqs.explanation: The aggregate pattern draws a transactional consistency boundary around an entity and its closely related objects; reaching outside that boundary (into Customer or Inventory) is exactly the cross-aggregate coordination that belongs in an application service instead. ORMs don't forbid cross-entity references outright, naming doesn't resolve the transactional/consistency concern, and the boundary matters specifically for state-changing operations, not just reads.
